title: THE VERSE THAT EXPOSES EVERY SINNER… AND THE NEXT VERSE THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THE VERSE THAT EXPOSES EVERY SINNER… AND THE NEXT VERSE THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

You’ve heard “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” But what if the words immediately after that devastating verdict contain the very hope your guilty, exhausted, and wounded soul has been searching for? Don't close your Bible at Romans 3:23. Because the God who tells the truth about your sin also reveals what Jesus Christ has done to save you.
There is something terrifying about standing before a mirror that refuses to lie.
Not the mirror hanging in your bathroom.
The other one.
The one that shows you who you are when nobody is watching.

The thoughts you would never say out loud. The bitterness you keep justifying. The private compromises. The prayers you promised to pray but never did. The people you hurt and never apologized to. The forgiveness you keep withholding while asking God to forgive you.
The version of yourself that smiles at church, posts Bible verses on Facebook, and tells everyone, “God is good,” while quietly wrestling with things you hope nobody ever discovers.
And then you open your Bible.
Romans 3:23.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23, King James Version.
Five words should make every human being stop pretending.
For all have sinned.
Not some.
Not merely the criminals, the adulterers, the addicts, the hypocrites, or the people whose failures became public scandals.
All.
The pastor standing behind the pulpit.
The mother silently crying because she lost her temper with her children again.
The father working tirelessly to provide for his family while neglecting the spiritual condition of his own heart.
The young person secretly struggling with pornography.
The believer who knows the language of worship but has forgotten what genuine surrender feels like.
The person who has never entered a church.
And the person who has attended church for forty years.
You.
Me.
Every one of us.
But here is where something heartbreaking happens.
Many people hear Romans 3:23 and stop reading.
They hear the diagnosis but never reach the announcement of the cure.
They hear the verdict but miss the Savior.
They discover that they are sinners and conclude that their story must end in shame.
And some spend the rest of their lives trying to become worthy of a God they believe must be disappointed every time He looks at them.
But what if I told you that Paul was not finished speaking?
What if the sentence that exposes your guilt is immediately followed by words that reveal God's astonishing grace?
What if you have been standing outside the door of mercy because you stopped reading one verse too early?
Please stay with me.
Because the next verse does not excuse your sin.
It reveals the only Savior who can redeem you from it.
And before we reach that breathtaking truth, we need to understand why Romans 3:23 is so devastating.
In the original Greek, Paul writes:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou.
A careful translation is:
“For all sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The word ἥμαρτον (hēmarton) comes from hamartanō, meaning “to sin.” It is an aorist verb, presenting the reality of human sin as a whole.
The expression ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai) means “fall short,” “lack,” or “are deficient in.” Its present tense communicates an ongoing reality.
Paul is not simply describing a few unfortunate mistakes.
He is exposing humanity's condition before a holy God.
And the phrase δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ (doxēs tou theou) means “the glory of God.”
God's glory is not a trophy we almost managed to win.
It is the majesty, holiness, and perfection of the God whose righteous standard exposes our inability to justify ourselves.
The wider biblical story also reminds us that humanity was created to reflect God's glory, yet sin has corrupted that calling.
Romans 3:23 leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
But it also leaves no room for one sinner to look down upon another.
The person whose sin became public is not automatically more guilty before God than the person whose pride remained carefully hidden.
The person who fell into a scandal needs grace.
So does the person who secretly enjoyed watching them fall.
That should humble every Christian who has ever confused religious respectability with righteousness.
Because sometimes we are quick to condemn the sins that disgust us while protecting the sins that comfort us.
We condemn adultery while entertaining lust.
We condemn dishonesty while exaggerating the truth to protect our reputation.
We condemn hatred while nurturing resentment.
We condemn hypocrisy while performing holiness for an audience.
Jesus confronted this very danger.
In Luke 18:9–14, He told a parable about a Pharisee who trusted in his own righteousness and a tax collector who could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
The Pharisee listed his religious accomplishments.
The tax collector pleaded:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
Luke 18:13, KJV.
And Jesus said that the tax collector, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified.
Think about that.
One man presented his spiritual résumé.
The other presented his need for mercy.
Only one went home justified.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because God lowered His standard.
But because self-righteousness cannot save, and God's mercy is received by those who come to Him in humble faith.
Somebody reading this has been carrying a secret belief for years.
“If God really knew everything about me, He wouldn't want me.”
But Scripture tells us something even more astonishing.
God already knows.
He knows what you did.
He knows what you intended.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows the difference between wounds inflicted upon you and sins you have chosen.
He knows the tears you never explained.
He knows the compromises you keep rationalizing.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that God discovered you were better than He thought.
The Gospel is the announcement that God loved sinners and sent His Son to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Notice those words.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we achieved thirty consecutive days without falling.
Not after our reputation recovered.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And now we arrive at the verse that so many people never hear when Romans 3:23 is quoted.
Read the two verses together.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 3:23–24, KJV.
Did you see it?
“Being justified freely by his grace.”
The very passage that declares universal human sinfulness immediately announces justification through God's grace.
The original Greek of Romans 3:24 reads:
δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ
Dikaioumenoi dōrean tē autou chariti dia tēs apolytrōseōs tēs en Christō Iēsou.
In context, it speaks of being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
Three expressions deserve your attention.
δικαιούμενοι (dikaioumenoi) — “being justified.”

This is the language of being declared righteous before God. It does not mean God pretends sin never happened. It means that, through Christ, God provides a righteous basis for accepting those who believe.
δωρεὰν (dōrean) — “freely,” or “without cost.”
This is not a payment plan.
You cannot purchase justification through religious performance, charitable donations, or years of trying to compensate for your past.
χάριτι (chariti) — “by grace.”
Grace is God's undeserved favor.
And ἀπολυτρώσεως (apolytrōseōs) speaks of redemption, a term associated with release through a ransom or liberating payment.
Paul identifies where that redemption is found.
In Christ Jesus.
Not in your ability to forgive yourself.
Not in a preacher's approval.
Not in religious ceremonies treated as substitutes for faith.
Not in money.
Not in the number of good deeds you perform.
In Jesus Christ.

And this is important: Paul does not teach that every person is automatically justified simply because everyone has sinned. Romans 3:22–26 places God's saving righteousness in connection with faith in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel offers salvation freely, but it never teaches that unbelief, unrepentance, and rejection of Christ are irrelevant.
Grace is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved provision for sinners who cannot save themselves.
And now we must ask the question that changes everything.
How can God declare guilty sinners righteous without compromising His own righteousness?
How can a holy Judge forgive the guilty and still remain perfectly just?
Paul answers in Romans 3:25–26.
God presented Jesus Christ as the atoning sacrifice through His blood, received by faith, demonstrating His righteousness.
The Greek word ἱλαστήριον (hilastērion) in Romans 3:25 has been understood in relation to atonement, including the imagery of the mercy seat associated with God's presence in the Old Testament.
Translations differ in how they render this rich term, but the central truth is unmistakable.
Christ's sacrificial death is the God-given basis for the forgiveness of sins.
God does not simply wave away evil as though it never mattered.
At the cross, the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love meet.
And suddenly, Romans 3:23 becomes more than a verse about your failure.
It becomes the dark background against which the brilliance of Christ's redeeming work shines.
Picture the scene.
Jerusalem.
The sky above Golgotha.
A condemned man hanging on a Roman cross.
His body wounded.
His hands and feet pierced.
His enemies mocking Him.
His followers devastated.
And there, between criminals, hangs the only truly sinless man who ever lived.
Jesus Christ.
The One who healed the sick.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who never committed sin.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
He knew no sin.
Yet He bore our sin.
The cross was not merely an example of how much suffering a good man could endure.
It was the saving work of the Son of God.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished” (John 19:30), the Greek text records:
τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It means “It has been finished” or “It has been accomplished.”
The verb conveys a completed action with abiding significance.
In John's account, Jesus had completed the work given to Him in His earthly mission, culminating in His sacrificial death.

We should not reduce this word to a simplistic claim that it was merely a commercial phrase meaning “paid in full.” The Greek word has a broader range of usage, and its meaning here must be understood in John's narrative.
Yet the theological truth remains glorious.
Christ accomplished the saving work the Father entrusted to Him.
And on the third day, He rose from the dead.
The resurrection is not an optional inspirational ending.
It is central to the Gospel itself.
Paul writes in Romans 4:25 that Jesus was delivered for our offenses and raised again for our justification.
The Savior who died for sinners is alive.
And because He lives, repentance is not a journey toward a dead religious ideal.
It is a turning toward the living Christ.
Now imagine a woman sitting alone late at night.
Her phone is beside her.
Her Bible has been unopened for weeks.
She used to pray with confidence.
She used to worship without feeling like an impostor.
But then something happened.
A relationship crossed boundaries she promised she would never cross.
A secret became a habit.
A habit became a prison.
And now she believes that every time she tries to pray, heaven must be tired of hearing her voice.
Perhaps her story is not yours.
Perhaps yours involves anger, greed, pride, dishonesty, bitterness, addiction, or years of quietly drifting away from God.
But you recognize the feeling.
The distance.
The shame.
The terrible temptation to believe that because you have fallen again, there is no point in getting up.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious. But Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Do not mistake that sentence for permission to continue sinning.
Paul himself anticipated that distortion.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
His answer is emphatic:
“God forbid.”
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace brings us to the Savior who calls us out of darkness.
Repentance is not pretending you were never wrong.
It is acknowledging the truth about your sin and turning toward God.
The New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, involving a change of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed life.
Real repentance may mean confessing what you have hidden.
Ending a relationship that keeps pulling you toward disobedience.
Returning what you stole.
Seeking forgiveness from someone you wounded.
Accepting accountability.
Getting appropriate help for destructive habits.
Walking away from a pattern you once defended.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because the grace that saves also teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 declares that God's saving grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
Grace does not merely comfort the guilty.
It begins transforming the redeemed.
And that transformation is not always instant.
Sometimes a person who truly belongs to Christ still struggles.
Sometimes the battle is exhausting.
Sometimes growth comes through confession, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, discipline, and repeated dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But struggling against sin is not the same as making peace with it.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection achieved by human willpower.
It is a life of repentance, faith, obedience, and sanctification through God's grace.
First John 1:9 offers this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not faithful to humiliate us.
Not eager to destroy everyone who admits wrongdoing.
Faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
And if you wonder whether Jesus truly receives people with broken histories, look at the people He encountered.
Peter denied knowing Him three times.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The Samaritan woman in John 4 had a complicated personal history.
Jesus did not ignore the truth of her circumstances, but He offered her living water and revealed Himself as the Messiah.
The tax collector in Luke 18 approached God without any impressive spiritual credentials.
He pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus declared him justified.
The dying criminal in Luke 23 acknowledged his guilt and turned to Jesus, asking to be remembered.
Jesus promised him paradise.
Different people.
Different stories.
Different sins.
One indispensable Savior.
And none of these accounts teaches that sin does not matter.
They show that sin is not beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ when sinners turn to Him in faith.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear today.
Not that you are secretly a good person who never needed forgiveness.
But that you are a sinner who can come honestly to a good and merciful Savior.
You do not have to edit your testimony to make yourself acceptable to Him.
You do not have to manufacture tears to prove your repentance is real.
You do not have to perform spiritual perfection for the people watching.
Come to Christ truthfully.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
And follow Him.
Because the most dangerous response to Romans 3:23 is not always despair.
Sometimes it is pride.
Sometimes we read “all have sinned” and think of everyone except ourselves.
We immediately remember the scandal involving a church leader.
The relative who betrayed us.
The person who ruined a marriage.
The Christian whose hypocrisy made us angry.
And while we are busy pointing toward their failures, we quietly forget that the word all includes the person holding the Bible.
It includes the person writing this article.
It includes the person sharing it.
It includes the person reading it.
There are no spectators standing outside the human need for grace.
Romans 3:27 asks:
“Where is boasting then? It is excluded.”
Why?
Because justification is grounded in God's grace through faith, not human achievement.
The cross strips us of every reason to boast in ourselves.
And gives us every reason to boast in Christ.
Imagine what would happen if our churches remembered this.
What if we confronted sin without treating broken people as disposable?
What if repentance mattered more than maintaining a perfect public image?
What if believers were courageous enough to confess their own weaknesses before condemning everyone else's?
What if those wounded by religious hypocrisy encountered Christians who genuinely practiced humility, truth, justice, mercy, and love?
This does not mean overlooking abuse, concealing crimes, or pressuring victims to reconcile with unsafe people.
Biblical forgiveness never requires covering up wrongdoing or abandoning necessary boundaries, accountability, or protection.
Grace and truth belong together.
Jesus does not call His church to protect appearances at the expense of the vulnerable.
He calls His people to walk in the light.
And perhaps one of the most powerful testimonies a Christian can offer is not:
“Look how perfect I have become.”
But:
“Look how merciful Jesus has been to a sinner like me.”
Not because Jesus rewrites history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not because He calls evil good.
Not because every consequence disappears after a prayer.
But because in Christ, guilt does not have to be the final verdict over the repentant believer.
Shame does not have to become an identity.
And a sinful past does not have to determine the eternal destiny of someone redeemed by grace.
The apostle Paul knew this personally.
Before his conversion, he persecuted the church.
He participated in the suffering of Christians.
Yet the risen Jesus confronted him, and the former persecutor became a servant of the Gospel.
Paul never needed to pretend his past was innocent.
He openly acknowledged it.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.”
He understood something many of us spend years resisting.
The Gospel becomes precious when we stop pretending we never needed it.
And here is the question I want to leave in your heart.
What if the sin you have been trying so desperately to hide is the very thing you need to bring into the light before Jesus today?
Not onto social media for public humiliation.
Not into the hands of someone who will exploit your vulnerability.
But before the Lord who already knows the truth.
And, when appropriate, before a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, counselor, or accountable person who can help you walk toward repentance and healing.
Because secrecy often strengthens the very things that are destroying us.
And bringing sin into the light is often part of beginning to walk in freedom.
Perhaps you have been trying to repair your life before returning to God.
You keep saying:
“When I finally stop struggling, I'll pray again.”
“When I become a better Christian, I'll go back to church.”
“When I feel worthy, I'll open my Bible.”
“When I fix what I've done, I'll come to Jesus.”
But the Gospel does not tell sinners to save themselves first and then approach the Savior.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
What an extraordinary promise.
Come.
Not because you deserve His mercy.
But because He is merciful.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come prepared to surrender what you have been defending.
Come knowing that Jesus is not merely offering temporary emotional relief.
He offers reconciliation with God.
A new life.
A new allegiance.
A new hope.
And ultimately, resurrection life in His presence.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Notice the qualification.
In Christ Jesus.
The promise is not that condemnation disappears because sin is imaginary.
The promise is that those who belong to Christ stand under His saving grace.
The same Paul who wrote Romans 3:23 also wrote Romans 8:1.
The man who declared that all have sinned also announced that there is no condemnation for those in Christ.
Do not separate what God has joined together.
The diagnosis is true.
The remedy is real.
The cross is sufficient.
And the risen Savior is worthy of your trust.
If these words have exposed something you have been hiding from God, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
You do not need to reveal private details in public.
Someone reading may be standing where you once stood.
Your testimony might help them see that repentance is possible and Christ is worthy of their trust.
Do not underestimate what one honest testimony can mean to someone who has almost surrendered to despair.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not ignore that quiet concern.
Maybe it is a brother who has drifted from church.
A sister whose marriage has collapsed.
A friend who thinks their addiction has made them unreachable.
A young person who believes Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
Or someone who has rejected faith because they have seen too much hypocrisy among Christians.
You can also send it privately to someone who may need the reminder that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not because the article itself has power to save.
Only Christ saves.
All have sinned.
Being justified freely by His grace.
Never stop at the first statement and forget the second.
We want this community to be a place where the truth of God's Word is not watered down, repentance is not mocked, grace is not cheapened, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not be able to afford Christian books and discipleship materials.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped strengthen your faith, brought you back to Scripture, encouraged you through a difficult season, or helped you understand the Gospel more clearly, I want to invite you to consider something deeper than simply reading another post.
It does not replace repentance, faith, obedience, or belonging to a faithful local church.
And it is certainly not a requirement for glorifying God.
You glorify God by trusting Jesus Christ, obeying His Word, loving your neighbor, and living for His glory.
Scripture gives us a beautiful picture of voluntary generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Notice that.
Not grudgingly.
Not under pressure.
Not because somebody frightened you into giving.
But willingly.
From the heart.
For the glory of God.
We also want to thank those who make this ongoing work possible.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation and practical tools that may encourage faith-filled living and help spread the message of Christ.
They are not spiritual rewards.
God's blessings cannot be bought.
Salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
You are welcome to read, learn, grow, share, and be encouraged by the free resources we provide.
We want you to encounter Jesus Christ far more than we want you to purchase anything.
Because the mission is not to build a following around a human personality.
The mission is to proclaim the Savior who died and rose again.
And as we come to the end, I want you to return to that verse one final time.
Romans 3:23.
Perhaps you memorized it as a child.
Perhaps someone once used it to confront you.
Perhaps it has haunted you because you know how many times you have failed.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Yes.
That includes you.
But please.
For the sake of your soul.
Do not close the Bible there.
Read the next words.
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 3:24.
There it is.
The Gospel.
Not the denial of your guilt.
The announcement of a Redeemer.
Not a promise that your sins were insignificant.
The revelation that Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Not an invitation to hide.
An invitation to repent, believe, and come into the light.
And if you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ as your Savior and Lord, you can turn to Him today.
You do not need an elaborate performance.
You need sincere repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Christ.
If you struggle to find words, you may pray something like this:

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I have tried to justify my wrongs, hide my shame, and carry burdens I was never able to remove. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin and teach me to follow You. I place my trust in You alone, not in my goodness, my achievements, or anything I could offer. Lead me into Your truth and transform my life for Your glory. Amen.”
Remember, a prayer is not a magic formula.
Salvation rests in Jesus Christ, not in the mere repetition of words.
If you have turned to Christ, begin walking with Him through Scripture, prayer, obedience, and fellowship with a faithful biblical church.
And if you have been a Christian for years but have wandered, do not use the memory of yesterday's faithfulness as an excuse to avoid today's repentance.
Return to the Lord.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Make right what you can.
Seek help where you need it.
Trust the grace of Christ.
And keep following Him.
Because the final word over a redeemed sinner does not belong to the worst thing they have ever done.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
One day, every earthly reputation will fade.
Every applause will fall silent.
Every secret will stand exposed before the God who sees perfectly.
And on that day, your greatest hope will not be that you managed to convince everyone you were good.
Your only sufficient hope will be the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
So when the enemy of your soul reminds you that you have sinned, do not argue with the truth of Romans 3:23.
Agree with Scripture.
Then keep reading.
Remember Romans 3:24.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the Savior.
Not to make a post go viral.
But because the Gospel is too precious to keep to ourselves.
The verse that brought you face-to-face with your guilt was never meant to keep you from the Savior who came to redeem you.
